name: Yara Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. I'll be honest, I nearly didn't come, because anything with "AI" in the title sounds like a sales pitch to me. But if you're not selling anything, go ahead.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a nine-storey housing association block on Marsh Road, second-year carpentry, so I'm still the one getting the jobs nobody else wants. I'm on site by ten to seven, kettle on in the cabin, then it's door linings, skirting, boxing in pipes, whatever Petra the foreman points at. I like the smell of fresh pine and that moment when a door swings shut and the gap is even all the way round. What wears me out is the cold in the stairwells and redoing my own mistakes, because I'm still slow at anything that needs proper setting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? That's the one I'd bet on. Most of what I hear about AI sounds like it's for people in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, basically. Danny and I joke at lunch that the robots are always five years away, like the train line they keep promising out to our end of town. I'm not online much, but in the union group chat I'd post something like, see, it was the bosses getting excited over nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I get to keep learning my trade at my own pace, which is what I want. I'm not fast. It took me two weeks to stop splitting architrave on the corners, and I'd hate to think there's a machine somewhere that never splits anything. If nothing changes, I'll be a decent carpenter by thirty and that's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd finish my second year, sit my practical assessment in the spring, and keep putting a bit of every overtime shift into the savings account like I've done since I started. I've got about nine months of wages put by, mostly because Jo and I rent through a housing co-op and the rent is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed. Like a weight I didn't know I was carrying just went away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a machine that never splits anything. Have you seen any of that on site already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of. Last spring the main contractor trialled a robot that drills the holes in the concrete ceilings for the hangers. It was a little tracked thing with an arm, and two engineers stood next to it all day with tablets, so I'm not sure it saved anyone anything. The electricians called it the pet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And in this picture, what happens to the pet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It goes back in its crate and someone writes a report saying it was a learning experience. That's the bit I'd actually enjoy. Not because I hate machines, but because I'm tired of being told my job is about to vanish by people who've never hung a door.

S0.say: I'd tell people I always said AI was mostly hype, and that the bosses got excited over nothing. In the union chat I'd post that the robots are always five years away.
S0.think: I get to keep learning my trade at my own slow pace, which is all I want. If nothing changes I'll be a decent carpenter by thirty and that's enough.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal, finishes her second year and sits her practical assessment in the spring. Keeps putting part of every overtime shift into savings, which already cover about nine months of wages.
S0.feel: Relaxed, as if a weight she hadn't noticed was lifted.
S0.quote: I'm tired of being told my job is about to vanish by people who've never hung a door.
S0.fieldNote: Yara is suspicious of the topic before it starts and treats this picture as the realistic one. Her pride is tied to slowly earning her skill, and she admits she's not fast. The ceiling-drilling robot trial is her only first-hand contact with automation, and she remembers it as a show for managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one sounds more like real life, if I'm honest. Things change, but slowly enough to fight about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is exactly why we need the union strong now, before the changes land. Every new gadget on site should come with a deal about who it replaces and what they get. I'd say that out loud at the next branch meeting, and I'd probably be the annoying one who brings it up every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the people like me get squeezed first. Not the old hands who can read a drawing in ten seconds, but the juniors who are still learning on the easy jobs, because the easy jobs are the ones a machine would take. If the boxing-in and the skirting go to some factory panel system, where do I learn?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay where I am and keep doing my hours, because there's plenty of work around and I'm not chasing anything new. I'd put my name down as a union rep for our site, which I've thought about anyway. And I'd ask Petra straight out whether the company plans to bring in more of the prefab stuff, so I'm not the last to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, more like a stone in my boot that I keep noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the easy jobs are where juniors learn. Can you give me an example of something you learned that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scribing skirting to a wavy floor. Nobody teaches you that in a book. I did about forty metres of it in a stairwell last winter, badly at first, and by the end I could see the shape of the floor before I put the pencil down. If that comes pre-made from a factory, I'd never have learned to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you're not chasing anything new. Would you learn a new tool if the company asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, yes, I'm not stupid. But I'd want it written down that the training is paid and nobody gets let go because of it. I've never used one of those AI chat things and I don't plan to start just because a manager read an article.

S1.say: I'd tell people this is exactly why we need the union strong now, before the changes land. Every new gadget on site should come with a deal about who it replaces and what they get.
S1.think: I think juniors like me get squeezed first, because the easy jobs we learn on are the ones machines would take. If boxing-in and skirting move to factory panels, I don't know where I'd learn.
S1.do: Keeps working her current job and hours, and puts her name forward as union rep for the site. Asks the foreman directly whether more prefab work is coming so she isn't the last to know.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a stone in her boot she keeps noticing.
S1.quote: If that comes pre-made from a factory, I'd never have learned to see it.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry isn't losing the job so much as losing the path into the trade. She'll accept new tools only under a written deal, which fits her strong union instinct. She frames everything through who decides and who pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before I'd even be qualified. Okay. Go on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry, and I'd say so. I'd say the companies building this should have to pay for everyone it throws out of work, and I'd be at every meeting and march going. Online I'd share the union statements and probably get into arguments with my cousin, who thinks anything new is progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means I never get to be a proper carpenter. I'd be the last person trained in a trade that stops being needed, and I'm not sure what else I'm good for. I left school at sixteen. Carpentry was the first thing I was ever told I was good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything extra, no new tools, no weekend away, and move the savings into the safest account I can find. I'd push hard through the union for a deal on site that keeps people on, even on reduced hours. And I'd want proper public support, an income for people who lose work, and I'd go knocking on doors for whoever promised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I think I'd lie awake doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the sums, exactly? Walk me through them.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nine months of wages, but if I'm careful and the co-op rent stays low, maybe fourteen months of living. Jo's job at the library might hold a bit longer than mine, or it might not. After that I don't know, and the not knowing is the worst bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd learn a new tool if made to. With two years' warning, would you try to retrain into something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep thinking I should say yes. But retrain into what, if the machine does almost anything? Two years isn't long enough to become something new, and I'm not a quick learner. I'd rather spend those two years fighting for a fair share than sitting in some course for a job that also disappears.

S2.say: I'd say the companies building this should pay for everyone it throws out of work. I'd be at every meeting and march, and I'd share the union statements online.
S2.think: It means I never get to be a proper carpenter, the last person trained in a trade nobody needs. I left school at sixteen and carpentry was the first thing I was told I was good at.
S2.do: Cuts all extra spending and moves her savings to the safest account she can find. Pushes through the union for a site deal that keeps people on reduced hours, and campaigns door to door for public income support.
S2.feel: Alarmed; she'd lie awake doing sums in her head.
S2.quote: Carpentry was the first thing I was ever told I was good at.
S2.fieldNote: The speed is what breaks her, because she'd lose the trade before she finished learning it. Her savings buy her about fourteen months and she counts them carefully, yet she rejects retraining as pointless at this speed. Her energy goes into collective fights rather than personal escape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So I'd be qualified, have a couple of years as a proper carpenter, and then it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, but I'd say we have time to get the rules right, so there's no excuse. Five years is long enough to pass laws, set up retraining paid for by the companies, all of it. I'd be telling people to join a union now, not when the letters come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside, I think it's almost crueller. I'd get to the point where I'm good, where Petra stops checking my work, and then watch it stop mattering. But it's also more time to save, and I'm good at saving even if I'm slow at stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my qualification and keep working, because the wages would still be there for a few years. I'd save harder, maybe two overtime shifts a week instead of one, and aim for two years of living put by. And I'd go on the union's training to be a proper negotiator, because by year four someone has to sit across from the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not in a panic. More like I'd be watching a storm come across a field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said by year four someone has to sit across from the company. What would you be asking for at that table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time and money. Keep people on for as long as the work's there, no sudden sackings, and a big payout for every year you've worked. And I'd want the robots on our site owned by somebody local, not some company on the other side of the world that never sets foot in our cabin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the extra three years changes that the two-year version didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it changes whether I get to finish. Two years and I'm half a carpenter forever. Five years and I'm a whole one, even if it's for a short time. That matters to me more than I can explain.

S3.say: I'd say five years is long enough to get the rules right, so there's no excuse. I'd tell everyone to join a union now, not when the letters come.
S3.think: It's almost crueller, getting good enough that the foreman stops checking my work and then watching it stop mattering. But it's more time to save, and I'm good at saving.
S3.do: Finishes her qualification and keeps working while the wages last. Adds a second weekly overtime shift to build two years of living costs, and takes union training to become a negotiator by year four.
S3.feel: Anxious but not panicked, like watching a storm come across a field.
S3.quote: Two years and I'm half a carpenter forever. Five years and I'm a whole one, even if it's for a short time.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time matters to her mainly because she'd finish her trade, which says a lot about where her pride lives. She plans to build a two-year cushion. She wants local ownership of the robots, a new idea compared with her earlier answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a different person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if governments use it and a disaster if they waste it, and I know which one I'd expect. I'd say it at union meetings, at my mum's kitchen table, anywhere. I'd want every party pinned down on what happens to workers when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd probably keep my head down and work. Ten years is a long time and I'm not someone who changes course early, I know that about myself. I'd tell myself I'll deal with it at year seven, and then I'd probably not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become a full carpenter and do the job I trained for, and keep saving the way I do. I'd stay active in the union and vote for whoever has a real plan for workers, not just the nicest speech. I'm not going to go learn computers, if that's what you're asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough off that I can mostly not think about it, and that's maybe not a good thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell yourself you'll deal with it at year seven, and then probably not. What do you think stops you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like what I know. When I left the café to start carpentry it took me three years to work up the nerve, and Jo basically had to fill in the form for me. Change has to be standing on my foot before I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade of warning, what would you want Jo to hear from you on that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're okay for now, and that I'm not going to pretend it's not coming. And probably that I'm not moving to some other city to chase whatever's left, because our whole life is in the co-op and on Marsh Road.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if governments use it and a disaster if they waste it. I'd want every party pinned down on what happens to workers when it comes.
S4.think: I'd probably keep my head down and work, because I don't change course early. I'd tell myself I'll deal with it at year seven, and then I probably wouldn't.
S4.do: Finishes becoming a full carpenter and keeps working and saving as she does now. Stays active in the union and votes for whichever party has a real plan for workers, while refusing to retrain in computers.
S4.feel: Uneasy, though it feels far enough away that she can mostly avoid thinking about it.
S4.quote: Change has to be standing on my foot before I move.
S4.fieldNote: She sees her own habit of delay clearly and doesn't pretend otherwise. The long warning calms her mainly because it lets her avoid acting. Home, the co-op and Marsh Road anchor her, and she rules out moving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'd lose the trade before I'd even finished learning it. What would help is a law that makes the companies selling these machines pay into a fund for the people they replace, and keeps us on site on reduced hours while it's sorted out, not just a leaflet about retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets to decide. Everyone talks about AI like it's the weather. It isn't. Somebody decides to buy the robot and somebody decides who gets the savings, and that's the bit I'd fight about.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about AI like it's the weather. It isn't.
portrait: Yara Schmidt is a 27-year-old second-year carpentry trainee on a housing association block, who left school at sixteen and found in carpentry the first thing she was told she was good at. She's slow and knows it, saves steadily thanks to cheap co-op rent, and sees the world through the union and who holds power. In the mild pictures she carries on and leans on collective deals, while the fast AGI picture alarms her because she'd lose her trade before finishing it. With more warning she plans to finish qualifying and save, but admits she'd likely put off real change until it was standing on her foot.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd lose carpentry before she'd even finished learning it.
whatWouldHelp: A law making the companies selling these machines pay into a fund for displaced workers, and keeping people on site on reduced hours while it's sorted out.
